Notice that the most precise results under cluster sampling, as suggested by comparing the
compositions of clusters 1 and 2, will be obtained when each cluster has a heterogeneous
composition, while the clusters tend to be similar. The estimate derived from stratified sam-
pling was near the true value of the population parameter because the units in each cluster
were all mixed up while similarity was maintained between clusters. The reverse is true for
stratified clustering, strata are internally homogeneous, while the strata themselves are as
heterogeneous as possible.
In practice, cluster sampling produces less precise estimates than a simple random sample of
the same size, since in actual studies one is often required to accept the clusters as they exist.
Usually these clusters will be relatively homogeneous.
Suppose the researcher wants to determine the type of activity and average time spent on
computing in the home on a daily basis. Image the potential cost of running this study using a
simple random sample. Why not use cluster sampling? Households in a single book are fairly

41.4.4 a lternative sampling methods
There are other sampling methods employed in practice. The following brief list provides
operational definitions for the alternative methods.
41.4.4.1 s ystematic s ampling
For the population of signs we would simply select a random number between 1 and int
(n/N), where n is the sample size, N is the population size, and int(_) is the largest positive
whole number less than or equal to the function’s argument. Then choose every int (n/N)
sampling unit from a starting point, say a value between 1 and n. Systematic random sam-
pling is based upon the concept of selecting elements from a randomly arranged sampling
frame according to ordered criteria. For a very large sampling frame and a large sample,
systematic random sampling is very inexpensive and direct plus very simple to implement.
41.4.4.2 d ouble s ampling
In the quest for a more cost effective and efficient sampling method for situations requiring
large samples and large sampling frames, a sample of a sample can be employed, or dou-
ble sampling can be used. For instances, a simple brief questionnaire could be utilized for
obtaining data on representative household occupations for a large population from a sample
of ten thousands of households. This process could then be administered a comprehensive
questionnaire, using the proportions of each occupational group in the larger sample, for
selecting a sample with sample size in the several orders of magnitude lower than for the
first questionnaire.
All of the sampling methods discussed so far rely on obtaining a random sample, there-
fore, you can rely on the Central Limit Theorem and the associated properties of the unit
normal distribution to determine the amount of sampling error in the sample. In order to
calculate the standard error, or the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of means,
it is necessary to evaluate the formula:

Think about the person-on-the-street interviews seen on local and national newscasts. In
accidental sampling sample units are selected on the basis of being available or being easily
included upon immediate selection.
Most of us have run into people in a mall carrying clipboards with attached questionnaires
stopping various people entering or leaving the mall. Usually, the mall pedestrian is pursued
by these people and asked to participate in some study; actually the mall pedestrian has been
sized up to see whether or not they are qualified for being selected for membership in the
sample. Purposive Sampling is useful in situations requiring efficient access to a target group.
Modal sampling is when you sample the most frequent case. Interviews of the ‘typical voter’
is an example of a modal sampling application. But what is a ‘typical voter’?
Panel of experts are common at national and /or professional meetings. This is a good
approach to elicit the views of individuals with specific expertise. Expert Sampling deals
with assembling a sample of individuals possessing demonstrable experience and/or exper-
tise within a domain.
Pollsters use quota sampling to predict the outcomes of elections. The sampling units are
selected on the basis of perceived categories within the population. In stratified sampling
the sampling elements are selected within the stratified groups. On the other hand, in quota
sampling the elements are selected within presumed subdivisions of the population.
41.5 s ampling e rrors
When sampling ensures that every sampling unit has a chance of being selected and the prob-
ability of selection is known, then the sampling errors are controllable. The following list points
out some important types that the researcher needs to be concerned about when gathering data:
1. reporting and processing errors,
2. non-response errors,
3. errors in sample selection, and unit sampling errors.

36615.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
36615.heading: 41.6 Field s tudies
36615.content:
41.6 Field s tudies
Imagine being asked to implement research on everyday events. For example, assume you
have been hired to study the cognitive activities of professional programmers in their corpo-
rate computing center.
How would you begin this study? What are we really trying to accomplish? We are attempt-
ing to understand how they resolve and solve problems during their daily activities, both on
an individual and team basis. What type of organizational structures formally and informally
are in place within the working environment?
It will probably take a considerable amount of effort to simply decide which aspects of the
personnel’s behavior to investigate, let alone determine hypotheses to test. These behaviors
involve individual and corporate team interactions.

36616.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
36616.heading: chapter 41 n Survey an D F I el D r e S earch n n n 531
36616.content:
chapter 41 n Survey an D F I el D r e S earch n n n 531
But how will we collect all this information? Based upon most of our everyday experiences
many of us would probably suspect:
1. use of photography to capture photos that can be immediately shared and analyzed.
2. take photographs every day of a sitting or artifact possibly photographs every day of a
team’s whiteboard – which could contain a list, or log, of an individual’s assignments
and other personnel with whom they interact.
3. use of video for recording meetings for future interpretation.
4. maintain written notes – a pocket notebook to use on a moments notice, a word
processor to organize your thoughts using an “outline” mode or writing observations
under continual recording and maintenance.
5. you could classify the systematically organized observations.
Basically, you would be starting to employ a collection of methods that include direct obser-
vation of naturally occurring events. Direct observation is where the event is observed as it
happens. Naturally occurring events are events that are not created, sustained, or discontin-
ued solely for research purposes. This type of research is referred to as Field Research. In
this section, the practices of field research will be discussed.
Through observation you would begin to collect data on the personnel’s activities and even-
tually formulate new hypotheses. Field research is suitable for exploratory and descriptive
goal finding studies.
Most of your time during a field study is bound to be through either recall or direct observa-
tion. In the proposed study, you would be examining how people solve problems and make
decisions in real work environments. By studying the daily events of the personnel in this
work environment, it would be best for you to not only observe but simultaneously, take part
in the events. After all, the best approach to understand problem solving, is to ‘learn it by
doing it’. This approach is called Participant Observation. Studies where you observe events
without participating in them, thus being as unobtrusive as possible, are called Systematic
Observation.
During the proposed study, it seems appropriate to collect data on observations of behavior
on the part of the software development team. However, imagine the insight to be gained by
collecting their individual reports of behavior.
Systematic information on the personnel’s daily activities could be obtained simply by asking
them to report their activities for a recent specified period of time. You could ask them open-
ended questions and record the answers, or create a time diary. Clearly, both of these tech-
niques require interviewing and recording skills. The time diary would keep data on when
an activity starts, ends, and its sequence with the other daily activities. More than likely for

36617.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
36617.heading: chapter 41 n Survey an D F I el D r e S earch n n n 531
36617.content:
your recording in the time diary, you will need to invent a coding scheme for the activities.
But when do you record the activities? The obvious answer is to record the subject’s behav-
ior the moment they are observed. This type of procedure is referred to as Instantaneous
Sampling.
532 n n n r e S earch Metho DS F or In F or M at I on Sy S te MS n ch apter 41
Just like it is important for students to take notes, participant observers must decide how
much detail to include in their field journals. If something happens, then you must post it in
the field journal. How often should you maintain the field journal? The obvious answer is at
every available opportunity. Often the difference between remembering and forgetting an
event is dependent on sketch notes in the field journal. Remember that the field journal is
the participant observer’s primary research tool.
Clearly field research involves the researcher following activities and observing through
questionnaires and interviewing. These events must be selected, recorded, coded, and inter-
preted. The field study is really an understanding process, both about the domain and about
the cognitive activities under study. The researcher wants to:
1. form hypotheses about the behavioral patterns observed,
2. make predictions, and
3. finally, verify the predictions.
The following article ‘The Observational Study of Behavior’, by J. Altmann published in
Behavior 48: 1–41, illustrates how data analysis of abstractions and the associated interpreta-
tions can be the primary effort in a field study. When studying this article it is important to try
to identify sources of error in the study. Observations need to be measured reliably, or con-
sistently, and they must be valid, in other words, do they measure what they are supposed to
measure. Otherwise you cannot describe events and test hypotheses about them. Inadequate
sampling could be present in a field study. Also the researcher should be very careful about
changing their minds about what to observe, this leads to inadequate sampling. Other error
sources are due to recording, observing, and interpreting observations.
A text on qualitative field research which serves as a manual to follow when conducting an
ethnographic project, complete with examples, is A Guide to Qualitative Field Research by
Carol Bailey published by Pine Forge Press, 2nd Edition (September 14, 2006). Another
reference, for the interested reader is The Observational Study of Behavior by J. Altmann
published in Behavior 48: 1–41.

Study Ethnographic Study of MSIS Student Project Team Dynamics, by Ronald S. King,
found on the textbook’s DVD. Problem-solving styles and interpersonal dynamics of project
teams are often critical dimensions of the ability of a team to function effectively. In order
to study the problem-solving styles of students enrolled in a graduate Database Adminis-
tration and Development class at the University of Mary Hardin-Baylor (UMHB) and to
track their intrateam interactions, the theory established by M.J. Kirton in 1976 was used
to determine the cognitive styles of the students. Students were categorized according to
adaption-innovation characteristics of the Kirton Adaption-Innovation Inventory. These cat-
egorizations were then applied to interpret the results of interviews from informants and the
team leaders, and about the abilities of project team members to work and communicate
with each other.

42.1 i ntroduction
This chapter is a proposal on how to build and evaluate models for solving problems, espe-
cially when applying the multiple regression approach. Basically the proposed steps are:
First specify the problem, complete with identifying and screening of the variables. The
chosen variables must be correlated to the problem under study and readily accessible. By
carefully studying a correlation matrix for all independent and dependent variables for cur-
rently maintained data, the researcher is allowed to run pilot tests on simple regression
models. These preliminary tests enable insight into future modeling efforts. This is also a
good time to establish goals for the project complete with estimates for project completion
requirements such as necessary time and cost.
Next a model, or several models to be followed, needs to be developed by selecting a best
representative model, using correlation analysis, the researcher should study the interrela-
tionships between various independent variables. Out of this effort, the researcher will be
able to select independent variables in regression equations, as well as transformed inde-
pendent variables that may be used in the final results. Study of residual plots should also be
performed at this time. Finally, once a useful model has been chosen, then procedures for
verification of the model and model maintenance should be started.
This chapter and the header article are an attempt to illustrate the model-building process.
Special emphasis is on procedures for selecting variables for a regression analysis as well as
choosing a best regression model for a specific study. The process follows a personal data
analysis methodology recommended by Katrina D. Maxwell in Applied Statistics for Soft-
ware Managers published by Pearson Publications, Inc. (2002). Maxwell’s text provides not
only a personal data analysis methodology, or a model building process, but illustrates the
process using actual corporate data to solve specific software productivity, time-to-market,
and maintenance problems.
42.2 s ample s tudy
Study Forecasting Gold Prices Using Multiple Linear Regression Method by Ismail, Yahya,
and Shabri, found at http://www.scipub.org/fulltext/ajas/ajas681509-1514.pdf. Both this arti-
cle and the material found in this chapter illustrate and outline the steps for constructing
linear models. Linear models tend to crystallize one’s thinking with regard to the variables
operating in an experimental situation. Models form the basis for the analysis and interpreta-
tion of data generated by the experiments. Therefore, the model should undergo a prelimi-
nary analysis as well as be validated.

36640.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
36640.heading: 42.3 Lessons Learned
36640.content:
42.3 Lessons Learned
It usually takes a number of years to collect enough software project data to analyze. Add
the software industry’s high job turnover rate, and more often than not, you will be analyzing
data that was collected by others. What methods should you use? What should you do first?
42.3.1 s tep 1: v alidate your data
Data validation is reviewing the data to determine that it is the right data for the
study and that the values are correctly specified and fit the variable’s scope.
Data validation is the most important step, as it is critical to verify that the specific data is
complete, accurate, and fit. Data is often assembled from various sources, and it needs to be
evaluated to make sure it was gathered correctly and that it adequately represents that for
which it was gathered.
A Judgment Analysis (JAN) study is used throughout this chapter for discussing model con-
struction. Consider the following study, which was generated by a research request from the
College of Business Administration at Omega University. The Information Systems Depart-
ment wanted to find and measure a set of criteria that would be descriptive of the doc-
toral candidate selection process by the IS faculty. This set of criteria would be descriptive
of the candidates’ success in the program. Selective procedures for doctoral candidates in
IS involve looking at many predictor variables; some of these variables are GRE popula-
tion, GMAT scores, Miller Analogies Test (MAT) scores, Strong Vocational Interest Blank
(SVIB), incoming GPA, and previous major field of study. The MMPI is also required for
each incoming doctoral candidate. However, in the past many of the doctoral graduates did
not take the MMPI. Because of this, the 13 subscales of the MMPI were not included in
the study. To describe the doctoral candidate selection process used by the IS faculty, three
questions had to be answered:
n How many distinct judgmental policies are presented among the IS faculty with
respect to what they consider the important cognitive and affective skills of an
outstanding graduate student?
n Which of the affective and cognitive skills being considered for each graduate do the
faculty deem most important?
n Which predictor variables used in determining admission to the program relate to the
captured judgmental policy or policies?

36641.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
36641.heading: 42.3.1.1 Statement of Problem
36641.content:
42.3.1.1 Statement of Problem
At present there seems to be a wide variety of methodologies available to capture and ana-
lyze judgmental policies where either the investigator is looking only at predictor variables
alone or there is one criterion variable and several predictor variables. The author has been
unable to find in the literature a methodology for capturing and analyzing judgmental poli-
cies where the investigator is looking at a set of criterion variables and a set of predictor
variables in conjunction. Therefore, the problem was to attempt to capture and analyze

judgmental policies of the IS faculty while looking at both a set of criterion variables and a
set of predictor variables.

36642.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
36642.heading: 42.3.1.2 Purpose
36642.content:
42.3.1.2 Purpose
The basic purpose of this study, which was service-oriented in nature, was to develop a
methodology for capturing and analyzing judgmental policies where the investigator is look-
ing at a set of criterion variables and a set of predictors in conjunction. This type of meth-
odology was needed so that the technique can be used to a great degree in judgmental
research.
42.3.2 s tep 2: s elect the variables and model
Variable and model selection determines what variables and relationships to study
to ensure all steps taken target the intended purpose of the study.
The purpose for variable and model selection is to determine what data we actually have and
the semantics of the data. What relationships could we study? What possible relationships
should we study? What relationships will we study first? Your answers will depend on the
overall goals of the analysis.

36643.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
36643.heading: 42.3.2.1 Operational Definitions
36643.content:
42.3.2.1 Operational Definitions
In this section, we provide definitions of various concepts discussed throughout this
chapter.
Ipsative JAN refers to the JAN approach in which the judges were using personal knowledge
of the capabilities of each IS doctoral graduate to suggest a rank. It is a way of quantifying
subjective opinions that yields more objective results.
The judges are only those faculty who have had the student as an advisee or student, or
worked on special projects with him and rated the student using the criterion instrument.
The judgmental evaluation procedure is the outcome of a rating process by a judge who has
been presented a series of variables on which he must base a decision. For example, how
does a judge involve effective thought processing when presented with a series of variables
on which he must base a decision?
Normative JAN refers to the JAN approach in which the judges were utilizing the predictor
variables to rank each IS student into one of seven categories.
A profile score is a profile that was defined as the set of ratings assigned by a judge to a spe-
cific IS doctoral student on the nine criteria, Y
i
, i = l, ... , 9.
Type A JAN is an analysis in which all the judges give judgments on the same subjects with
respect to the same criterion variable and predictor variables.
Type B JAN is an analysis in which the judges do not judge the same subjects (different
judges could judge a different number of subjects also) with respect to the same criterion
variable and predictor variables.

36645.heading: 42.3.2.2 Questions Answered
36645.content:
42.3.2.2 Questions Answered
The questions answered were subdivided into two general populations. The first population
of concern pertains to how well the methodology answered the questions of the IS research
request. These questions are as follows:
n How many different judgmental policies exist within the IS Department concerning
what constitutes an outstanding IS doctoral graduate?
n Which of the affective and cognitive skills being considered for each graduate do the
faculty deem most important?
n What kinds of information that they now collect are important indicators of a
graduate’s ability to succeed as an IS employee?
The second population of concern involves interpretation of computer outputs. The major
questions that were considered are as follows:
n What type of judgmental policies are captured?
n Is it possible to determine whether or not each judge is a “good” judge?
n How many judgmental policies are captured?
n What are the most important predictor and criterion variables?
n What is the relationship between the criteria and predictors of importance?
n Is the procedure for analyzing a captured policy an intuitive or a statistical process?

36648.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
36648.heading: 42.3.2.4 Judgment Analysis
36648.content:
42.3.2.4 Judgment Analysis
The Judgment Analysis technique is useful for identifying the rating policies existing in a
board or committee of judges. With this technique, each judge makes a judgmental decision
on one common criterion variable on which he is given a common predictor set profile on a
set of judges to determine how many different evaluation policies exist in the group. Next,
a multiple regression analysis can be made to determine the composition of each captured
policy.
The JAN procedure consists of two basic stages. In the first stage, a least-squares solution
of a multiple regression equation is computed for each judge, which predicts the criterion
decision he has made. It answers the question of how consistent the judge is in his use of
specific variables in arriving at an overall decision by giving his decision-making equation
and the R
2
, the square of the multiple correlation coefficient, from his multiple regression
analysis. A high R
2
indicates that he has a policy and was consistent in expressing it through
his criterion decisions.

36649.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
36649.heading: chapter 42 n a Metho D o L o G y for Mo D e L c o NS truct I o N n n n 543
36649.content:
chapter 42 n a Metho D o L o G y for Mo D e L c o NS truct I o N n n n 543
Next, a hierarchical grouping procedure is initiated that allows the grouping of individual
judges according to some objective function by similarity of their decision-making equations
in this case. Groupings are selected that yield the smallest decrease in ability to predict the
criterion from knowledge of which individual judges are in a particular group (loss in R
2
).
The first step in the grouping procedure reduces the number of equations by one. The two
judges whose decision-making equations are most similar are grouped together as a unit and
all other judges are left ungrouped. From the set of ungrouped judges, the process then
selects a judge whose decision-making equation is most similar to that of the grouped judges
and groups him with them as a unit. The number of judges remaining in the ungrouped set
is reduced by one at each step of the process until all judges have been grouped into a single
unit. At each step of the grouping process, an examination of the loss of predictive efficiency
allows the investigator to identify the number of various judgmental policies that exist.
If a single policy is characteristic of the whole collection of judges, it can be determined at
the final stage of grouping. If a joint policy does not exist, arbitration of the criterion by the
whole group may yield a joint policy.
Judgment analysis has been extensively used by the United States Air Force to analyze indi-
vidual and group judgments and to formulate common or overall judgmental policies. A large
amount of this type of work has been done by Ward, Bottenberg, and Christal. Bottenberg
and Christal
1
were originally responsible for the mathematical and computer program devel-
opments in the field.
2

42.3.3 s tep 3: p erform preliminary analyses
Preliminary analysis is a review of the data to become more familiar with its parts,
descriptions, and relationships, in order to make sure it will not violate any of the
assumptions the statistical tests are built on.
The purpose of the preliminary analysis is to check that the assumptions underlying the sta-
tistical tests are true. You need to objectively look at the data and decide on the goal for the
study. You must determine which of the variables collected has an influence on achieving this
goal. The preliminary analysis will utilize different types of graphs, tables, correlations, and
other statistical tools.

The IS Department had its first doctoral graduate 10 years earlier. Since then, not including

36665.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
36665.heading: 42.3.4.3 Strategy Used for Obtaining Data
36665.content:
42.3.4.3 Strategy Used for Obtaining Data
Procedure 1
Out of the approximately 500 sets of ratings obtained on the criterion instrument, 40 were
randomly selected.
Procedure 2
Each of the 16 members of the IS faculty were asked to do a modified Q-sort on the 40 sets of
ratings. Each set of ratings was called a profile. They were asked to compare the 40 profiles
against one another and place them in seven groups. Group 7 would represent those pro-
files they considered the best of the group of 40 and group 1 would represent those profiles
they considered the poorest in the group of 40. Groups 2 through 6 lay on an ordinal scale
550 n n n r e S earch Metho DS for I N for M at I o N Sy S te MS n ch apter 42
between one and seven. The only restrictions were that each judge must place at least one
profile in each of the seven groups. Hopefully, this forced the 12 judges to think along the
whole continuum. The instrument and the instructions used for the Q-sort were presented
to the IS faculty in a training session before they actually conducted this part of the study.
Procedure 3
After the judges completed the rankings, a Type A JAN was run to determine the number
of judgmental policies. The decision as to the number of policies existing was based on the
following consideration: Any judge who was unable to identify at least one significant factor
is failing to relate any predictor variable set to any criterion variable.

42.3.5 s tep 5: c heck the model
Checking the model is verifying that the variables of the final model do not violate
assumptions upon which the model is based. This involves careful determination
that the variables are correctly distributed and standard errors are random, as well
as looking at any other stringent variate requirements.
The purpose of checking the model is to make sure that the assumptions underlying the
statistical tests used have not been violated In some experimental designs, we may reduce
the variance of the estimator and increase the information by either reducing the variance
(noise) or increasing the sample size (volume of the signal).
In practice, the assumptions for a linear model are rarely satisfied. The experimenter does
not know all of the important variables in a process nor does he know the true functional
relationships. Therefore, the function chosen to fit the true relation is only an approximation,
and the variables included in the experiment form only a subset of the total. The random
error is thus a composite of error caused by the failure to include all of the important process
variables as well as the error in approximating the function.
